title: Uruguay’s Left Seeks Lessons from Lula’s Victory
gist: EIU economist Nicolás Saldías argues Lula's reelection in Brazil gives Uruguay's Frente Amplio only a short-term boost: Orsi's approval is at a record-low 24% amid weak growth (0.9% est. 2026) and homicides up 13% to their highest since 2018, while 45% of Uruguayans would accept a nondemocratic government that solves problems. Lessons for the left: social media mobilization and fickle late-deciding voters ahead of the 2030 race.

themes.theme: Orsi's unpopularity and the affability gap

insights.claim: Uruguayan President Yamandú Orsi's approval hit a historic low of 24% in October 2026 per Cifra, with 57% disapproving - the lowest of any Uruguayan president in their second year since 2000.
insights.speaker: NICOLÁS SALDÍAS
insights.so_what: Weak governing mandate limits Orsi's capacity for reforms; political risk for Frente Amplio continuity.
insights.quote: Orsi’s approval rating reached a historic low of 24% in October

insights.claim: Orsi's personal favorability (41%, and 68% among Frente Amplio voters) far exceeds his job approval, revealing a perception gap between him as an affable leader and an effective one.
insights.speaker: NICOLÁS SALDÍAS
insights.so_what: Pragmatic course correction is possible given residual goodwill.
insights.quote: the ongoing perception gap among the electorate between Orsi as an affable leader and an effective one

insights.claim: Lula's victory in Brazil is unlikely to alter the Orsi government's fortunes at home beyond a short-term boost.
insights.speaker: NICOLÁS SALDÍAS
insights.so_what: Do not read regional leftist momentum as improving Uruguayan political fundamentals.
insights.quote: apart from a short-term boost, Lula’s victory is unlikely to alter the government’s fortunes at home

themes.theme: Uruguay's weak growth and Brazil/Argentina spillovers

insights.claim: Uruguay's GDP grew 1.8% in 2025 and is estimated to grow only 0.9% in 2026, with EIU forecasting acceleration to 2% in 2027 partly from higher agricultural output on more favorable climate.
insights.speaker: NICOLÁS SALDÍAS
insights.so_what: Uruguay's growth recovery hinges on agriculture; a weak base for sovereign and local assets.
insights.quote: GDP expanded by 1.8% in 2025 and is estimated to grow by a mere 0.9% this year

insights.claim: A slowdown in Brazil, where economic forecasts have turned decidedly negative after Lula's win, and potentially in Argentina due to pre-election political jitters, could dent Uruguay's 2027 growth prospects.
insights.speaker: NICOLÁS SALDÍAS
insights.so_what: Uruguay's outlook is exposed to neighbor risk; watch Brazil post-election forecasts and Argentina's election.
insights.quote: Economic forecasts in Brazil have taken a decidedly negative turn following the results.

themes.theme: Lessons from Lula: incumbency, social media and fickle voters

insights.claim: Lula's win was the first example in many years of an incumbent left-wing Latin American government winning reelection, achieved despite voter concerns over crime, low growth and high cost of living.
insights.speaker: NICOLÁS SALDÍAS
insights.so_what: Breaks the regional anti-incumbent pattern - an update for Latin American election-risk models.
insights.quote: it was the first example in many years of an incumbent left-wing government winning reelection

insights.claim: Lula's victory showed the left adopting social media communication strategies that had been the domain of the right, and Uruguay's left can leverage organized unions and student movements to mobilize and create viral content.
insights.speaker: NICOLÁS SALDÍAS
insights.so_what: Social-media campaign capacity is becoming a decisive electoral variable on both sides.

insights.claim: Polls are becoming less accurate and surprises more common as partisan identification weakens and many voters - especially younger ones - decide just before elections based on issues and personalities.
insights.speaker: NICOLÁS SALDÍAS
insights.so_what: Widen error bands on Latin American election polling; price higher surprise risk.
insights.quote: polls are becoming less accurate and political surprises are more common than in the past

insights.claim: Because Orsi cannot run for reelection, the Frente Amplio may benefit for the 2030-35 term; potential candidates include Alejandro Sánchez, economy minister Gabriel Oddone and vice president Carolina Cosse.
insights.speaker: NICOLÁS SALDÍAS
insights.so_what: Candidate choice (e.g. market-friendly Oddone vs. others) will shape Uruguay's policy outlook.

insights.claim: Former President Luis Lacalle Pou, who left office with 53% approval, is widely expected to run and will be hard to frame as a radical; Uruguay's right is unlikely to adopt Milei-style radical free-market policies or a Bukele-style security agenda.
insights.speaker: NICOLÁS SALDÍAS
insights.so_what: Uruguay's political center of gravity stays moderate, supporting policy stability whichever side wins.
insights.quote: It will be very difficult to frame him as a radical, given that voters already know how he governs.

insights.claim: Uruguay recorded 312 homicides in January-September 2026, up 13% year on year and the highest level since the 2018 peak, despite a crime reduction plan launched in March.
insights.speaker: NICOLÁS SALDÍAS
insights.so_what: Rising crime is the dominant political issue and a growing governance risk.
insights.quote: homicides reached 312 over the January-September period, which is up 13% from the same period last year

insights.claim: Security is the top concern for 55% of Frente Amplio voters versus 26% citing the economy (Factum, mid-September), and Uruguay's homicide rate is significantly higher than Argentina's or Chile's despite similar development.
insights.speaker: NICOLÁS SALDÍAS
insights.so_what: Even the left's base prioritizes crime, pressuring the government toward tougher policy.

insights.claim: Interior minister Carlos Negro rejects mano dura, calling tougher penalties 'punitive magical realism,' even as public fatigue grows.
insights.speaker: NICOLÁS SALDÍAS
insights.so_what: Government-public mismatch on crime policy may cost the Frente Amplio politically.

insights.claim: Latinobarómetro finds 45% of Uruguayans would accept a nondemocratic government if it resolved the country's problems, and Bukele is their most favorably viewed foreign leader; Costa Rica's Bukele-style turn warns that even full democracies can backslide if crime goes unresolved.
insights.speaker: NICOLÁS SALDÍAS
insights.so_what: Even Latin America's strongest democracies carry rising institutional-erosion risk - relevant to sovereign risk premia.
insights.quote: 45% would accept a nondemocratic government if it resolved the country’s problems
